name: Sugar Hill Records
ownershipStory: Founded in 1979 by Sylvia and Joe Robinson, who had run All Platinum before it. Sugar Hill put rap on record first and dominated it for about five years, using a house band rather than DJs and assembling acts rather than signing them. It signed a distribution deal with MCA in 1983 that collapsed into litigation. The label filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in November 1985 and stopped operating around 1986, when the Robinsons sued MCA for fraud. That suit settled in 1990. Rhino bought the masters in 1995. The Englewood studio burned down in 2002.
hook: The label that proved rap could be sold, and set the industry's habits around it in the process.
blurb: Sugar Hill worked out how to turn a live Bronx party form into a three-minute product, and it is the first full example on this map of a label shaping the music rather than just appearing in the credits. Instead of recording a DJ, it had a house band replay the music. Instead of signing a real crew, it put a group together itself, and it was willing to push songs the artists themselves did not want. It worked: 'Rapper's Delight' sold millions. Those choices shaped both how recorded rap sounded and who got credit for it. For about five years Sugar Hill was where rap records came from. Then a distribution deal with a bigger company went wrong, the lawyers took over, and the label closed in 1986, the first case of a pattern the map will hit again and again.
